props.title: Entrapment
props.initialSlug: Master thief and sexy protégé plan ultimate heist

sections.content: Entrapment (1999) exemplifies the sleek heist thriller renaissance of the late 1990s, following the success of The Thomas Crown Affair (1999) and Ocean's Eleven (2001). Catherine Zeta-Jones and Sean Connery's electric chemistry drives this glossy cat-and-mouse game, with their 39-year age gap becoming a controversial talking point upon release. The film's elaborate heist sequences, particularly the iconic laser-beam corridor scene, influenced countless subsequent films like Mission: Impossible 2 (2000) and After the Sunset (2004).

sections.content: Director Jon Amiel's approach to filming the heist sequences set new standards for the genre. The Malaysian Petronas Towers climax particularly stands out, predating the real-world height exploitation of Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol (2011) by over a decade. The film's focus on high-tech security systems and their vulnerabilities echoes earlier works like Sneakers (1992) while influencing later entries like The Score (2001).

The insurance investigator angle puts Entrapment in conversation with classics like To Catch a Thief (1955) and modern entries like The Insurance Man (2003). Zeta-Jones's Virginia "Gin" Baker character subverts typical femme fatale tropes, instead presenting a competent professional whose motivations remain deliberately ambiguous until the final act. sections.content: Entrapment marked a crucial transition point between analog and digital heist films. While earlier entries like Thief (1981) focused on physical safecracking and alarms, this film bridges the gap to purely digital capers like Swordfish (2001) and Blackhat (2015). The millennium bug subplot, though dated now, captures the Y2K anxiety permeating late 90s techno-thrillers.
